lesson.title: Capstone: Build a Peer-to-Peer File Sharing System
lesson.summary: This capstone has you build a system where peers exchange files directly with each other rather than through a central server, using hash functions to verify content integrity and NAT traversal techniques to actually connect peers that each sit behind their own home router.
lesson.body:
Build an application where multiple peers can share files directly with one another. A file is identified by the hash of its content, not by its filename, so that a download can be verified as correct byte for byte, and so that identical content shared by different peers is automatically recognized as the same file. Most of the peers in this system sit behind their own home router doing network address translation, exactly as they do in real life, so connecting them to each other is not automatic, and making it work is a large part of the point of this project.

This is a genuine departure from the client-server model that almost every other project in this course has used. In the peer to peer model, a participant acts as both a client and a server to other participants at the same time, requesting chunks of a file from some peers while serving chunks it already has to others. There may still be a lightweight coordination server, often called a tracker, whose only job is helping peers find each other, but the actual file data moves directly from peer to peer rather than funneling through any central server. Build the coordination piece first: a simple tracker that peers register with and that hands back a list of other peers currently sharing a given file.

Hash functions do the integrity work in this system. Rather than trusting a filename or trusting that a peer sent you what they claimed to, split each file into fixed size chunks, compute a hash of each chunk, and verify every chunk you download against its expected hash before accepting it. This has a very practical payoff: if you download a large file as many small chunks from many different peers in parallel, and one peer turns out to be slow, unreliable, or outright malicious and sends you a corrupted chunk, the mismatched hash catches it immediately, and you can simply re-request that one chunk from a different peer instead of discarding and redownloading the entire file. Reassembling all the verified chunks and checking the hash of the complete file at the end gives you an overall integrity guarantee on top of the per chunk one.

The genuinely hard part of this project, and the part most worth taking seriously, is NAT traversal. Because most peers are behind a NAT device by default, they do not have a public, directly reachable address, which means two ordinary peers usually cannot just open a direct connection to each other the way two public servers could. STUN solves the first half of this problem: it lets a peer ask an external server what its own address and port look like from outside its own NAT, and two peers can exchange that information, typically via the tracker, and then both attempt to open a connection to each other at roughly the same time, a technique commonly called hole punching, that succeeds in a large share of real world NAT configurations. It does not always succeed, though, since some NAT and firewall configurations are restrictive enough to block it no matter what. TURN is the fallback for exactly that case: a relay server that both peers connect to and that simply forwards traffic between them, at the cost of that traffic no longer being a true direct connection.

Build this project in stages. Get two peers on the same local network exchanging a file directly first, with hash verification working correctly on both ends. Add the tracker so peers can discover each other beyond a single local network. Only then take on STUN based hole punching for the common case, with a TURN relay as the fallback when it fails. By the end, you will have combined a data integrity concept, hash functions, with a distributed architecture concept, the peer to peer model, and two deeply practical connectivity concepts, NAT traversal and STUN and TURN, that most engineers do not really internalize until they try to build something that has to work on real home networks, not just inside a clean lab environment where every machine has a public address.
